title: Krishna Reveals His Universal Form
story:
Duryodhana had been brought back into the assembly, and he stood before his father and the assembled kings still stiff with defiance. It was then that Krishna turned to him, and the tone of the court changed.

'From delusion, O Duryodhana, you regard me as alone,' Krishna said. 'It is for this, O you of little understanding, that you seek to make me a captive after vanquishing me by violence. Here, however, are all the Pandavas, and all the Vrishnis and Andhakas. Here are all the Adityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus, with all the great Rishis.'

And with that, the slayer of hostile heroes burst into loud laughter. It began as the laugh of a man amused by a child's boast, and it grew until the air of the hall seemed to thicken with it.

And as he laughed, the laughter became something else. From his body, which blazed like a fire, issued myriads of gods, each of lightning effulgence, each no bigger than a thumb. On his forehead appeared Brahman; on his breast, Rudra. On his arms appeared the regents of the world. From his mouth issued Agni, the Adityas, the Sadhyas, the Vasus, the Aswins, the Marutas, with Indra and the Viswedevas. Myriads of Yakshas, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas also came forth from him, of the same measure and form. From his two arms issued Sankarshana and Dhananjaya — and Arjuna stood on his right, bow in hand, while Balarama stood on his left, armed with the plough. Behind him stood Bhima and Yudhishthira and the two sons of Madri; before him were all the Andhakas and the Vrishnis, with Pradyumna and other chiefs, bearing mighty weapons upraised. On his countless arms were seen the conch, the discus, the mace, the bow Saranga, the plough, the javelin, the Nandaka — every weapon that is named, all shining with effulgence and upraised for striking. From his eyes and nose and ears, from every part of his body, issued fierce sparks of fire mixed with smoke; from the pores of his skin, sparks like the rays of the sun.

And these were not signs or symbols. They were there — gods and yakshas and heroes and weapons filling the assembly — so that the court of the Kurus became, for that moment, the meeting-place of all the worlds at once.

And the court of the Kurus beheld what no court of men had beheld. All the kings closed their eyes, their hearts affrighted — all except Drona, and Bhishma, and Vidura, and the greatly blessed Sanjaya, and the Rishis possessed of the wealth of asceticism, for the divine Janardana gave them divine sight on that occasion, so that they could bear to look. Many of the kings hid their faces; some covered their eyes with their hands; even the bravest among them could not raise their gaze.

In the sky above the hall, celestial drums beat, and a shower of flowers fell upon him. The whole Earth trembled, and the oceans were agitated. The wonder did not stay within the hall; it reached outward, to earth and ocean, as though the whole world had been summoned to witness what the court of the Kurus had provoked. And all the denizens of the earth were filled with great wonder, though few of them knew why.

Duryodhana had wanted to seize a man. What stood before him now, blazing from every pore, filling the hall with gods and weapons and fire, was what the four conspirators had proposed to bind with their hands. The boast had been answered not with a threat but with a revelation — the disclosure of what, all along, had sat before them through the peace negotiations, patient, and had been mistaken for a negotiator.

Then the vision withdrew. That tiger among men, that chastiser of foes, drew back the divine and highly wonderful and auspicious form, and was himself again — Krishna, the messenger of the Pandavas, seated quietly in the assembly of the Kurus, as though nothing at all had happened. The gods, the weapons, the fire — all of it had come from him, and all of it had returned to him, and what remained was the quiet figure the court had grown accustomed to, as though the two could not be the same person, and yet were.

In the ringing silence, the kings slowly opened their eyes.
reflection: Krishna answers a threat of capture not with a display of power aimed at the plotters, but with the simple truth of what he is. The vision is not a weapon; it is an unveiling. And it is telling that only those with some purity — Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Sanjaya, the Rishis — could bear to look, as though the sight itself demanded something of the seer.
next_story_tease: The court was still reeling when Krishna rose to go, and the blind king, shaken, hurried to protest that he was powerless.
hero_scene: Krishna laughs in the Kuru court while his body blazes — myriads of thumb-sized, lightning-bright gods streaming from him, Arjuna at his right and Balarama at his left, while the kings of the earth cover their eyes.
